summary: You produced a correct brute-force pair-checking solution and were careful to avoid using the same element twice by iterating j from i+1. However, you missed an edge-case expectation (empty/no-solution should return [] rather than raise) and you did not move from O(n^2) to the expected O(n) hash-map approach given the 1e5 constraint.

test_results.summary_note: Passed most tests but failed the empty-input edge case due to raising ValueError instead of returning an empty list.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Core logic correctly finds a valid pair when one exists, and the loop bounds (j = i+1) prevent reusing the same index twice.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Your function behavior didn’t match the test contract for empty/no-solution input: you raised an exception, which caused the failing edge test (expected []). Add an explicit return [] for empty input and for the not-found path when the platform expects a value, not an exception.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You restated the problem accurately (two distinct indices) and chose a straightforward baseline approach quickly. You also correctly reasoned about duplicates being fine because indices differentiate them.
dimensions.what_to_improve: You recognized the O(n) hash-map approach but didn’t pivot to it despite having time left and despite constraints that strongly signal it. Build the habit: once you have a correct baseline, immediately evaluate constraints and upgrade the approach before submitting.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You clearly narrated your plan (start brute force, optimize if time) and explained your implementation choices (inner loop starting at i+1). You also stated time/space complexity correctly for your implementation.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When prompted about unusual inputs, you dismissed edge cases too quickly and submitted without verifying behavior against potential platform expectations. A stronger close-out would be: explicitly list edge cases you’re handling (empty, no-solution, duplicates, negatives) and ensure the return contract is satisfied.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You correctly identified your solution as O(n^2) time and noted the hash map optimization to O(n).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Per the answer key and constraints (n up to 1e5), O(n^2) is not the expected approach. You should implement the hash-map pass-by-pass (store value->index, check complement) as the default for Two Sum unless explicitly constrained otherwise.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: The code is short, readable, and avoids common pitfalls like using the same element twice. Control flow is simple and easy to follow.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Raising ValueError as the default path reduced robustness and failed the platform’s expectation. Also, given constraints, leaving the brute-force version as final code is a maintainability/performance risk; prefer the canonical O(n) implementation for production-quality submission.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You implemented the baseline solution without step-by-step guidance and independently articulated complexity tradeoffs.
dimensions.what_to_improve: The single general hint (“consider unusual inputs”) was a clear prompt to validate edge behavior, but you still submitted without checking empty/no-solution handling. When hinted, pause and concretely test or reason through at least 2–3 edge inputs before finalizing.

thinking_and_logic: You took a correct baseline route: check all pairs (i, j) with j > i to ensure distinct indices, returning once the sum hits target. Your reasoning about duplicates was correct in the context of index-based answers. The main gaps were (1) aligning output behavior with the judge’s contract for empty/no-solution (tests expected []), and (2) not upgrading to the standard one-pass hash-map approach that matches the constraint-driven expected complexity.
code_assessment: The nested-loop implementation is clean and logically correct for cases where a solution exists and where raising on failure is acceptable. Test evidence shows it fails when input is empty because it throws ValueError rather than returning an empty list. Additionally, the final implementation remains O(n^2), which is not suitable for the stated upper bound and is flagged by the answer key as a known pitfall even though performance tests happened to pass here.

next_steps.action: Implement the canonical one-pass hash map solution for Two Sum
next_steps.why: It meets the expected O(n) time under large constraints and is the standard pattern interviewers want to see.
next_steps.how: Iterate i, x over nums; let c = target - x; if c in seen: return [seen[c], i]; else set seen[x] = i. Return [] at the end if not found (if the platform expects a value).

next_steps.action: Add a 30-second “edge-case contract check” before submitting
next_steps.why: You lost a test due to return/exception mismatch on empty input, even after a prompt to consider unusual inputs.
next_steps.how: Before final submit, explicitly run through: empty list, single-element list (if allowed), no-solution scenario, duplicates (e.g., [3,3], target 6), negatives. Confirm what to return ([], None, exception) matches the problem/judge.

next_steps.action: Use constraints as a decision gate for whether brute force is acceptable
next_steps.why: n=1e5 makes O(n^2) infeasible in principle, even if small tests pass.
next_steps.how: After restating the problem, immediately compute worst-case operations for your approach; if it’s > ~1e7-1e8, switch to a better pattern (hash map/two pointers/sorting) before coding.

patterns_to_study: return-contract vs exception handling in coding platforms
encouragement: Your baseline reasoning is solid and you already know the right optimization; focusing on edge-case contract checks and defaulting to the O(n) hash-map pattern will make this an easy full-pass next time.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Let me restate: I need two distinct indices whose values sum to the target. I'll start with the straightforward approach — check every pair with two loops — and optimize if there's time.
Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
One of the visible tests failed — the empty input case. You raised an error instead of returning an empty list.
Ah, I see. I assumed there's always a solution because of the constraints, so I raised. I'd need a guard for empty or no-solution inputs.
What's the complexity of your solution?
Two nested loops, so O(n squared) time and constant space. I know a hash map would make it O(n) but I didn't get to it.
